grits-with-cheese-fat-added.title: Grits with Cheese and Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Grits with cheese and added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of cooked grits mixed with grated cheese and a small amount of vegetable or butter fat. It offers a creamy, cheesy flavor combined with the nutty notes of the grain.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grits are made from ground corn and have been a staple in Southern cuisine for centuries.
Cheese adds calcium, protein, and a rich umami taste to the dish.
The added fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin D and K2 found in cheese.
Corn grits contain antioxidants like lutein that support eye health.
Ready‑to‑eat grits are convenient for quick meals without the need for cooking.

items.title: Good source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Grits provide steady energy and are easier to digest than many whole grains.

items.title: Provides protein and calcium
items.content: Cheese contributes high‑quality animal protein and calcium for bone health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The product supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which support metabolism.

items.title: Enhanced vitamin absorption
items.content: Added fat helps the body absorb fat‑soluble vitamins present in the cheese.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Corn grits are low in saturated fat, and the modest amount of added fat can be chosen as a heart‑healthy oil.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: The cheese component may trigger reactions in people sensitive to milk proteins or lactose.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Added fat increases the calorie count, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese often contains salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should be aware.

items.title: Potential gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: While grits are naturally gluten‑free, processing facilities may handle gluten‑containing grains.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the package. It can be enjoyed as a snack, mixed into salads, used as a filling for sandwiches, or warmed in the microwave for a hot meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in the original sealed package or an airtight container. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if you notice off‑flavors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Lima beans are large legumes obtained from the dried seeds of Phaseolus lunatus, a plant native to tropical and subtropical regions. They have a creamy color, a mildly sweet flavor, and a dense, buttery texture when cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lima beans are sometimes called “butter beans” because of their smooth texture.
When stored properly, dried beans can keep for 2–3 years.
Ancient cultures in Mexico and the Andes used lima beans in ceremonial dishes.
They are high in starch, making them a popular thickener for soups and stews.
After drying, beans may appear green (young) or yellow (mature).

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked lima beans provides about 15 g of protein, making them a valuable source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of folate (vitamin B9)
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Contains potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals help regulate blood pressure and support muscle function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Beans raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Present in dried beans and can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting lessen its effect.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Beans may cause bloating in sensitive individuals; gradual introduction to the diet helps.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Raw lima beans contain lectins that are destroyed by cooking; they should never be eaten uncooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried lima beans should be soaked for 6‑8 hours and then boiled for 45‑60 minutes until tender. They can be added to soups, stews, salads, purees, and vegetarian patties. They also make a creamy hummus when blended.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For very long storage (over a year), keep them in the refrigerator or freezer.

content.title: About
content.content: Pepperoni pizza is an Italian‑style dish popular in restaurants and fast‑food outlets. A thin or crispy crust (type 3399) is topped with tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and slices of spicy cured sausage called pepperoni.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “pepperoni” comes from the Italian “peperone,” meaning sweet pepper, though in the U.S. it refers to a spicy pork‑beef sausage.
Pepperoni pizza became one of the best‑selling pizza varieties in the United States during the 1970s.
Traditional pizza is baked in a wood‑fired oven at 400–500 °C, giving the crust a distinctive aroma and crunch.
A “double pepperoni” version doubles the meat layer for an extra‑intense flavor.
Some regions drizzle honey or barbecue sauce on the pizza for a sweet‑spicy contrast.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pepperoni and mozzarella provide a substantial amount of protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Pepperoni contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 from the meat supports nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Mozzarella is a good source of calcium, important for bone health.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pepperoni and prepared sauces often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Processed meats and cheese contain saturated fats that, in excess, may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk proteins should avoid traditional mozzarella‑topped pizza.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some sauces use MSG, which can cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pepperoni pizza is usually served hot, sliced into wedges. Fresh basil, a drizzle of olive oil, or extra spices can be added to taste. For extra crunch, the crust can be briefly reheated in an oven or grill.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore crust crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Ranch dressing fat free is a classic American sauce based on buttermilk but without added fats. It retains the characteristic creamy taste with hints of herbs, garlic and spices while providing minimal calories and virtually no fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ranch dressing was created in the 1950s in the United States as a salad dressing.
The fat‑free version appeared in the early 2000s as consumers sought lighter options.
Classic Ranch is commonly used as a dip for vegetables, chicken nuggets and french fries.
The fat‑free formula usually contains buttermilk, vinegar, spices, dry milk solids and flavor enhancers.
Ranch is the best‑selling sauce in the U.S. by volume.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Fat‑free Ranch provides about 30–40 kcal per 30 ml, making it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: The buttermilk base supplies live cultures that support gut health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Dairy components deliver modest amounts of riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides calcium
items.content: Buttermilk is rich in calcium, which helps maintain strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Reduced sodium in some versions
items.content: Certain brands offer a low‑salt formulation, beneficial for blood pressure management.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Contains dairy proteins and may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to milk.

items.title: Artificial additives
items.content: Some products use flavorings and preservatives that could be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort even with small amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fat‑free Ranch works well as a salad dressing, vegetable dip, chicken breast topping, or dip for baked potatoes. It can also be spread on sandwiches or used in marinades for a gentle flavor boost.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2 °C–4 °C. After opening, consume within 2–3 weeks. Do not freeze, as the texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: A waffle is a light, crisp baked good made from a batter of flour, eggs, milk and sugar. Frozen plain waffles are sold as ready‑to‑bake portions that retain a golden colour and crunchy exterior after heating in a toaster or oven.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Waffles originated in medieval Europe and were originally cooked in specialized iron plates.
In the United States waffles became popular in the early 20th century thanks to mass production and electric waffle irons.
Freezing allows waffles to stay fresh and retain their crisp texture for several months.
There are many flavour variations: classic, berry‑filled, chocolate, nut‑topped, etc.
Waffles are often used as a base for desserts such as waffle cake or waffle sandwiches.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Waffles provide quickly digestible carbs that give an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The batter is typically enriched with vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which support metabolism.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: Eggs in the batter contribute a modest amount of animal and plant protein.

items.title: Calcium and iron
items.content: Milk adds calcium, while whole‑grain flour contributes a modest amount of iron.

items.title: Low fat (when made with skim milk)
items.content: Many frozen plain waffles are prepared with minimal oil, making them less calorie‑dense than fried versions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Most ready‑made waffles contain added sugar, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or those limiting sugar intake.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional waffles are made from wheat flour and are not suitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Ingredients often include eggs, milk and sometimes nuts, requiring caution for those with food allergies.

items.title: Potential over‑eating
items.content: The crisp texture and sweet taste can encourage rapid over‑consumption.

items.title: Texture changes if overheated
items.content: Over‑heating can make the waffle overly hard and dry.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen waffle in a toaster, oven or microwave until golden. Serve with honey, fruit sauce, butter, yogurt or cream cheese. Add fresh fruit, nuts or chocolate chips for extra flavour.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen waffles in their original packaging in the freezer at –18 °C. After opening, reseal the bag tightly to prevent moisture and odor absorption. Properly stored, they remain good for up to 6 months.
